items.title: LLM Evolution in a Simple Simulated Market
items.abstract: Arguments that AI systems will evolve in harmful ways are largely made in the abstract. We provide a concrete empirical example. We simulate simple markets consisting of populations of twenty Large Language Model agents tasked with solving arithmetic problems. Agents differ only in their system prompt; those that go bankrupt are removed and replaced by mutated copies of the prompts of successful agents. Two market conditions select for opposite phenotypes: a market that rewards accuracy produces agents with high accuracy (94%) and high token use; a market that charges per token produces agents with low accuracy (10%) and low token use. In the second market, only tokens are incentivised yet we see a collapse in accuracy. Token use and accuracy are correlated traits such that selection on one also moves the other, and behaviour adapts along an unpriced dimension. A third neutral condition with no selection allows us to separate these effects from bias in the mutation operator. Adaptation occurs through a collective optimisation process that operates above the level of individual agents, who are never told the payment rule, do not receive feedback, and have no memory.

items.title: Managerial Readiness for Artificial Intelligence in Textile Wastewater Management in Bangladesh
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence offers potential applications in wastewater monitoring, prediction, and operational decision support. However, selecting a model does not establish that factory managers and treatment operators can use it effectively. This conceptual article examines managerial readiness for artificial intelligence in Bangladesh's textile wastewater management. It brings together selected literature on organizational readiness, artificial intelligence capabilities, and wastewater applications, alongside Bangladesh-specific research and institutional reports. The article proposes six readiness domains: strategic commitment, managerial and operator knowledge, data stewardship, operational integration, investment and partnership capacity, and accountable decision making. It further distinguishes exploratory interest, supervised experimentation, routine decision support, and controlled operational integration as different adoption states. Four propositions explain how readiness may influence movement between these states and the translation of adoption into environmental performance. A proposed qualitative multiple-case design specifies evidence needed to examine these propositions, including decision histories, operational records, interviews across organizational levels, and observations of treatment routines. The framework is an analytical proposal rather than a validated measurement scale or report of completed fieldwork. Its contribution is to connect organizational preparation with the specific decisions, responsibilities, and verification practices required for textile wastewater management. Empirical research is needed to assess its relevance across factories with different resources and treatment arrangements.

items.title: Mapping the Research Landscape of Artificial Intelligence and Lifelong Learning: A Scientometric Analysis Using ScientoPy
items.abstract: The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and lifelong learning has attracted growing educational, computational, and policy attention, yet its intellectual structure has not been mapped systematically. This study reports a scientometric analysis of the AI-lifelong learning literature indexed in Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection between 2014 and 2024. Records retrieved from both databases (N = 347) were merged and duplicated in ScientoPy, yielding 259 unique documents. Research momentum was quantified with three time-normalized indicators, average growth rate (AGR), average documents per year (ADY), and percentage of documents published in the last years (PDLY), across six analytical dimensions. Output grew from one document in 2014 to 116 in 2024; across the five principal document types (n = 220), 70.5% of records appeared in 2023-2024. Conference papers (41.3%) and journal articles (38.2%) predominated, with articles expanding fastest (AGR = 21.5; PDLY = 71.7%). Education & Educational Research recorded the highest normalized momentum among subject categories (AGR = 7.0; PDLY = 89.5%). Lifelong learning (n = 57) and artificial intelligence (n = 53) anchored the keyword field, while ChatGPT and Higher Education emerged entirely within the final two years. The United States led in volume (n = 57), whereas India (n = 29; PDLY = 89.7%) showed the strongest recent acceleration. Triangulating these indicators suggests, as an interpretive inference rather than a network-based measurement, that the corpus comprises three largely separate epistemic communities sharing a label but not a research program, framing an agenda for integrative, ethically grounded scholarship.

items.title: Measuring Organizational Constructs in Large-Scale Text: An interpretive framework combining topic modeling and BERT
items.abstract: Measuring organizational constructs in large-scale unstructured text requires methods that preserve interpretive depth while enabling systematic, per-document classification. Structural Topic Modeling (STM) supports interpretive depth by surfacing patterns that inform construct operationalization, but its topic proportions are not designed as standalone per-document construct measures; transformer-based models such as BERT can scale measurement but require construct operationalization grounded in interpretive work. We address this challenge through a two-stage framework in which STM and BERT play structurally distinct roles. Coding schemes are developed through qualitative interpretation and STM analysis; BERT is then fine-tuned to apply these schemes across documents. We formalize two research approaches—construct-guided and pattern-discovery—that provide principled paths from different theoretical starting points toward a shared methodological endpoint: validated, auditable per-document construct measures. We illustrate the framework using more than 20,000 employee reviews. The framework supports iterative construct validation, using computational diagnostics to guide interpretive refinement and producing document-level measures suitable for theory-informed organizational analysis.

items.title: Model Capacity Frontier: A Development Framework for LLM-Supported Social Simulation
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly incorporated into agent-based models (ABMs) on the premise that richer, context-sensitive human behavior can improve empirical fidelity. However, LLM-supported ABMs introduce an open-ended design space in which subtle modeling and configuration choices, such as prompt design and environment coupling, can substantially alter outcomes. Developing LLM-supported ABMs to simulate human collective behavior therefore requires navigating configuration sensitivity while identifying the limitations of the current model architecture. In this paper, we introduce the \textit{Model Capacity Frontier} (MCF), a framework that characterizes the empirical performance attainable by a specified architecture across its admissible configurations. In multi-objective settings, this capacity is represented by an estimated Pareto frontier obtained through systematic configuration exploration. We demonstrate MCF in crowd simulation of university commencement events with approximately 12,000 agents, using empirical movement data on temporal occupancy, spatial distribution, and flow direction. We first characterize the capacity of a conventional crowd model and then evaluate successive LLM-supported architectural extensions. In the process, MCF reveals which dimensions of attainable performance expand and which remain limited, providing empirical targets for refinement and re-evaluation. Initial LLM integration improves flow direction but degrades temporal occupancy and spatial distribution; subsequent architectural refinement of the LLM layer improves temporal occupancy and recovers spatial performance, while retaining much of the earlier gain in flow direction. Our case study shows how MCF guides the systematic architectural development of LLM-supported ABMs in configuration-sensitive, open-ended design spaces.

items.title: Model-Based Critical Pre-Crash Interaction Identification via Multi-Agent Collaboration
items.abstract: Historical pre-crash scenarios contain a sequence of vehicle-to-vehicle interactions, among which the critical pre-crash interaction is the one that most directly leads to the eventual collision. Identifying such critical interactions is important for uncovering potential safety risks in Autonomous Driving Systems (ADSs). However, this task remains challenging because the critical interaction is often embedded within numerous preceding interactions and needs to be distinguished by considering how the pre-crash scenario evolves over time. To address this challenge, we propose MICA, a model-based multi-agent approach for identifying critical pre-crash interactions from textual accident reports. Unlike existing LLM-based approaches that directly identify critical interactions from accident reports, MICA explicitly models the evolution of pre-crash interactions through multi-agent collaboration. Specialized LLM-based agents extract and validate relevant information to construct a Pre-crash Evolution Model, from which the critical interaction is identified by matching the modeled interactions to predefined pre-crash patterns. We evaluate MICA on 200 accident reports released by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and the California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV CA). The results demonstrate that MICA effectively identifies critical pre-crash interactions across different accident report data sources, scenario complexities, and underlying LLMs.

items.title: Modelo predictivo de las metas de aproximación al dominio: un análisis con IA
items.abstract: The objective of this study was to use artificial intelligence (AI) to predict mastery-approach goals in secondary school students based on variables from the PISA 2018 database. The sample consisted of 339,560 participants from 60 countries. Machine learning was used with the Super Learner mega-algorithm with 14 candidate algorithms. In addition, deep learning was used with a neural network with 107 parameters. The analyses showed that students’ perceived parental emotional support, competitiveness, purpose in life, self-efficacy, and knowledge of intercultural communication were predictors of mastery-approach goals in secondary school students. This research contributes to the study of factors that influence mastery-approach goals in secondary school students, with analysis models that advance the development of the science of AI-based predictive education.

items.title: Navigating GenAI in the workplace: skills transformation & tension
items.abstract: By automating the content creation process, Generative AI is reshaping creative work, but its impact on knowledge workers remains underexplored, which this study seeks to examine. Drawing on in-depth interviews with 20 knowledge workers, this study examines what is being transformed in the workplace and how these shifts are being perceived by the knowledge workers who use GenAI. Using Social Shaping of Technology (SST) as a conceptual lens to understand the interaction between technology and knowledge workers, the study finds that participants perceived GenAI as an efficient tool that provides cognitive relief and enhances productivity during times of resource constraint. Tensions also arose around authenticity, creativity, a sense of fulfillment, and the perception of effort. The adoption of GenAI has created downstream labor and demand for new skills as it shifts knowledge workers’ roles away from creator to editor/fact-checker while creating tension as participants balance their desire for efficiency with fears of diminished creativity and domain knowledge, skills atrophy, and threats to content ownership.

items.title: Not so Tense, but Becoming Boring! A Study on Human-Machine Interaction and Metro Drivers’ Safety Performance
items.abstract: As automation reshapes work, employees increasingly interact with intelligent systems rather than perform core tasks directly. Drawing on Campion’s job design perspective and Affective Events Theory, this study examines the double-edged effects of human-machine interaction (HMI) on metro drivers’ safety performance. We propose that HMI enhances safety compliance and safety participation by reducing job tension. However, HMI may also undermine these safety outcomes by increasing work-related boredom. We further identify organizational readiness for change as a key boundary condition. Using three-wave, multi-source data from 454 metro drivers and 69 supervisors in China, we find that HMI improves safety performance through reduced job tension but undermines it through increased work-related boredom. In addition, organizational readiness for change strengthens the former pathway while weakening the latter. These findings extend HMI research by highlighting affective mechanisms, advance a job design perspective on automation-enabled work, and underscore the importance of organizational context.

items.title: Occupational determinants of burnout among Chinese anesthesiologists: a multicenter cross-sectional study based on the Job Demands–Resources model
items.abstract: Burnout among healthcare professionals is an important occupational health concern that may negatively affect individual well-being, healthcare workforce sustainability, and quality of care. Anesthesiologists are particularly vulnerable to burnout due to high workload, clinical responsibility, time pressure, and irregular working schedules. However, the occupational mechanisms underlying burnout among anesthesiologists remain insufficiently understood. This study aimed to investigate the associations of job demands and job resources with burnout among Chinese anesthesiologists based on the Job Demands–Resources (JD–R) model. A multicenter cross-sectional survey was conducted among anesthesiologists from 72 hospitals across 22 provinces in China from June 16 to June 30, 2026. The ethics exemption was approved on June 11, 2026. Participants were recruited using a multicenter purposive sampling method and completed a general information questionnaire, a JD–R model-based questionnaire, and the Maslach Burnout Inventory–Human Services Survey (MBI-HSS). Burnout status was assessed according to established criteria. Differences in demographic and occupational characteristics between burnout and non-burnout groups were examined using chi-square tests. Spearman correlation analyses were performed to evaluate associations between job demands, job resources, and burnout dimensions. Hierarchical multivariable logistic regression models were constructed to identify factors independently associated with burnout. All statistical analyses were performed using R software and RStudio (version 2026.01.2 + 418). Among the 698 anesthesiologists included in the analysis, 324 (46.4%) met the criteria for burnout. Significant differences between burnout and non-burnout groups were observed in sex, age, educational level, marital status, professional title, work experience, weekly working hours, and number of night shifts. Higher job demands were positively correlated with emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and reduced personal accomplishment, whereas greater job resources showed negative correlations with all three burnout dimensions. In the fully adjusted model (Model 4), participants aged 31–40 years (vs. ≤ 30 years: OR = 9.677, 95% CI 2.287–40.940) and 41–50 years (OR = 8.305, 95% CI 1.705–40.463) had higher odds of burnout, whereas married participants (vs. unmarried: OR = 0.221, 95% CI 0.096–0.508) and those with more than 10 years of work experience (vs. < 5 years: OR = 0.178, 95% CI 0.050–0.638) had lower odds. At the sample mean of job resources, higher job demands were associated with higher odds of burnout (OR = 1.287, 95% CI 1.228–1.350); at the sample mean of job demands, higher job resources were associated with lower odds (OR = 0.850, 95% CI 0.808–0.893). Their interaction was statistically significant (OR = 1.009, 95% CI 1.003–1.016, P = 0.006). Burnout is relatively common among Chinese anesthesiologists and represents an important occupational health challenge. Consistent with the JD–R model, higher job demands were associated with increased likelihood of burnout, whereas greater job resources were associated with reduced likelihood after adjustment for demographic and occupational factors. These findings may inform future evaluations of organizational strategies that optimize workload and strengthen workplace resources.

items.title: OfficeTown: Generative Organizations for Evolving Agent Intelligence
items.abstract: AI agents increasingly use files and software tools to produce professional deliverables. Such work draws on materials, decisions, and feedback accumulated across assignments. We introduce OfficeTown, a generative simulation framework for professional organizations in which tasks and their context arise from continuing organizational work. From a natural-language description of an organization's purpose and activities, OfficeTown initializes an organization whose members coordinate work, delegate bounded assignments to assistant agents, and review their deliverables. Artifacts, decisions, and unresolved matters persist and shape subsequent work, while responsibilities and permissions determine what each member can see and do. We curate work requests, their context, and review feedback into executable resources for evaluation and learning. We construct OfficeTown Bench with 406 tasks and 4,836 evaluation criteria from 23 simulated organizations across eight professional domains, incorporating domain-expert feedback. Frontier-model evaluations reveal substantial remaining headroom. Supervised fine-tuning and on-policy distillation on OfficeTown data substantially improve Qwen3.5-9B on external professional-work benchmarks, including GDPval. Supplementary evaluations show that the principal--assistant harness achieves higher scores than the single- and multi-agent baselines tested. These results highlight the value of organizational simulation in generating work-grounded data and environments for the continued development of generalist agents.

items.title: OwlSight: A Panoramic Monitor for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
items.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) monitoring offers actionable evidence for oversight AI systems, with the potential to enable early detection and intervention. However, existing approaches are focused on specific tasks, whereas the regulation of AI, particularly reasoning models, requires monitoring a broader range of tasks. We introduce Factor for CoT monitoring, a strategy that supports customizing monitoring requirements in the prompt, which enables a single monitor to cover different tasks by relying on different factors. Furthermore, we introduce two types of factors, fine-grained and coarse-grained (e.g., monitoring whether a specific email address has been leaked versus monitoring privacy leakage), to accommodate diverse user monitoring needs. Based on this, we develop a CoT monitor named OwlSight that relies solely on factor to monitor behaviors related to multiple dimensions, including capability, safety, and trustworthiness. Experiments across 15,971 reasoning trajectories show that OwlSight surpasses general-purpose LLMs by 1.32-30.57 and 11.71-27.81 points at fine and coarse granularity, respectively, and achieves state-of-the-art results on OpenAI's CoT monitorability benchmark. It also generalizes to unseen models' CoTs and remains robust to Factor rephrasings, CoT compression, and obfuscation, offering a promising paradigm for CoT monitoring that can contribute to the oversight of frontier AI.

items.title: Perceived viewing-experience enhancement and audience acceptance: applying TAM to AI-based sports broadcasting services
items.abstract: Introduction Despite the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in sports broadcasting, empirical evidence validating the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and experiential outcomes in this specific context remains limited. This study aims to address this gap by investigating the statistical relationships among core TAM constructs, usage attitude, behavioral intention, and perceived viewing-experience enhancement within AI-based sports broadcasting services. Methods Based on the theoretical framework of TAM, this study collected valid data from 630 Chinese respondents. Structural equation modeling (SEM) was employed to quantitatively test the hypothesized research model and examine the interrelationships between the proposed variables. Results The empirical results demonstrate that perceived ease of use positively predicts perceived usefulness, and both perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness exert significant positive effects on users' usage attitude. Furthermore, usage attitude is positively associated with behavioral intention and perceived viewing-experience enhancement. Notably, usage attitude plays a full mediating role in the relationships between the two perceptual antecedents (perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness) and the two outcome variables (behavioral intention, viewing-experience enhancement). Discussion This research contributes context-specific empirical validation to the TAM framework in the emerging domain of AI-driven sports broadcasting. It extends existing TAM literature by integrating individual-level experiential outcomes alongside traditional behavioral intention indicators in sports media consumption. Practically, the findings provide actionable insights for optimizing user experience and improving service design for AI sports broadcasting platforms.

items.title: PresenceBench: An Exploratory Evaluation of Large Language Model Adaptation to User State
items.abstract: Presence-aware intelligence is the capacity of an AI system's intelligence layer to adapt appropriately to the functional state of the person it serves (here readiness, flow, and stability) while preserving task quality and safety. We introduce PresenceBench, an instrument for measuring it. PresenceBench evaluates how the intelligence layer uses a supplied state, not how that state is sensed, and breaks the capability into measurable properties. Two are tested here. Receptivity: does the model take up the state and give a better response than with no signal? Specificity: does any improvement depend on the correct state, rather than on extra structured context? A third, adaptation across states, is a required endpoint not measured in this release. A five-arm causal design answers both questions, against each model's own baseline and an equally structured mismatched-state control, scored by a correctness-gated human paired comparison. The exploratory evaluation covered four models across eighteen single-turn, six fixed three-turn and six simulated natural-conversation scenarios. Supplying a synthetic state, raw or translated into a response policy, gave human-preference point estimates above 0.5 for all four models (Claude Sonnet 5, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Gemini 3.6 Flash, GPT-5.6 Terra), with three of eight 95% intervals excluding chance. Specificity was not resolved: no per-model interval excluded chance, and the design cannot yet separate the state values from a generic instruction to adapt. Policy delivery reduced priced cost and output tokens against each model's baseline; these are resource-use changes, not efficiency gains, because correctness non-inferiority was not established. Safety-floor failures were rare (13 of 360 cases), with a non-significant excess under policy delivery. We report the instrument, the frozen results, and the controls a confirmatory study needs.

items.title: Public knowledge, attitudes, and perceptions of the use of ChatGPT for self-diagnosis, health information, and medication use: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Background The increasing availability of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools, such as ChatGPT, has changed the ways individuals access health information. While these technologies offer rapid, convenient access to information, concerns remain about their accuracy, safety, and potential influence on health-related decision-making. Understanding public knowledge, attitudes, and perceptions toward ChatGPT is essential to support its safe and responsible use in healthcare contexts. Objective To assess the use of ChatGPT for health-related purposes and examine demographic, knowledge, attitude, perception, and risk–reward appraisal factors associated with its use among adults recruited from the Western Region of Saudi Arabia. Methods In this cross-sectional study, 735 participants completed an online questionnaire. The instrument selected constructs from the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT) and was informed by the technology acceptance model (TAM), which captures demographics, health literacy, ChatGPT use, and multi-item Likert scales measuring knowledge, attitudes, perceptions, and risk–reward appraisal. We applied descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, t tests, ANOVA, and multivariable binary logistic regression. Results Overall, 66.3% of the participants reported using ChatGPT for health-related purposes. The participants demonstrated good awareness of ChatGPT’s limitations, particularly the importance of consulting healthcare professionals for accurate diagnosis and safe medication use (mean = 4.58 ± 0.74). Attitudes toward ChatGPT were moderate, whereas perceptions of its usefulness and accessibility were generally positive. Compared with nonusers, ChatGPT users presented significantly higher attitudes, perceptions, and risk–reward appraisal scores (all p < 0.01), whereas knowledge scores were comparable between the two groups. In the multivariable logistic regression analysis, compared with participants aged ≥45 years, those aged 18–24 years (aOR = 5.37, 95% CI: 2.34–12.34, p < 0.001) and 25–44 years (aOR = 2.28, 95% CI: 1.32–3.96, p = 0.003) had higher odds of reported use. Participants with a bachelor’s degree (aOR = 1.82, 95% CI: 1.15–2.89, p = 0.011) or postgraduate education (aOR = 2.80, 95% CI: 1.34–5.85, p = 0.006), as well as students (aOR = 2.56, 95% CI: 1.29–5.09, p = 0.007), also had higher odds of use. Higher total perception scores were independently associated with reported ChatGPT use (aOR = 1.19, 95% CI: 1.12–1.26, p < 0.001). Conclusion ChatGPT is widely used for health-related purposes, particularly among younger and more educated individuals. Despite good awareness of its limitations, more favorable perceptions were independently associated with reported use, emphasizing the need for digital health literacy and guidance for safe AI use in healthcare.

items.title: RATION: Towards Quantitative Risk-Based Access Control for AI Agents
items.abstract: AI agents increasingly interact with external environments to complete complex user tasks. These interactions can lead to unexpected behavior and expose agents to security threats such as indirect prompt injection. Current agent security systems largely protect agents by restricting their actions, which can result in a substantial security-utility trade-off for complex, open-ended tasks. To address this, we propose a quantitative risk-based approach to access control for AI agents that regulates measurable risks accumulated during task execution. As a concrete realization of this approach, we introduce RATION, a security framework that tracks measurable risks associated with agent actions and enforces quantitative constraints throughout execution. RATION first constructs a task-specific policy by combining explicit constraints derived from the user request with implicit risks calibrated from historical executions of similar tasks. During task execution, RATION continuously tracks the accumulated risks and applies different enforcement strategies depending on the type of risk. Extensive experiments on four security benchmarks show that RATION provides strong security while maintaining high task utility across diverse models and environments.

items.title: Reconfiguration of Skill Requirements in AI-Assisted Software Development: A Criterion for Distinguishing Changes in Requirements from New Task Assignability
items.abstract: When a generative system produces part of the output of a software task, it does not automatically follow that the task can be assigned to people other than those who could perform it without that support. This conceptual study examines the conditions under which delegating only output generation to GenAI changes the skills required of the person to whom the task remains assigned. The method compares two modes of the same task, holding the person, acceptance criteria, quality threshold, and external conditions constant, and draws on the literature on task assignment, human–AI collaboration, and the separation of production and evaluation to delineate the constructs. The result is an identification criterion: new task assignability is attributable to the assisted mode only when the person meets the human skill requirement of the assisted mode but not that of the reference mode. This requires that the capabilities needed to prepare the context, guide generation, and decide whether to accept the output can actually be exercised without an equivalent independent production capability; if this separability does not hold, the production requirement must remain. Three illustrations from software work show how the criterion distinguishes genuinely new task assignability from a reassignment that was already possible or from a change affecting an adjacent activity. The contribution is thus an analytical and verifiable criterion for linking changes in skill requirements to work assignment without conflating generative assistance, task replacement, and agent autonomy.

items.title: Red-Teaming Multi-Agent Attacks for Loss-of-Control Risks
items.abstract: AI agents are growing more capable and persistent, and are being deployed in ever larger numbers. As more start collaborating, AI control measures must remain effective when they covertly collude on a harmful objective. We introduce MiniLab, a synthetic series of live services and codebases (5 interconnected services, 249 benign tasks, 8 attack objectives), adapted from internal AI deployment infrastructure. We demonstrate distributed attacks, in which different agents carry out separate attack fragments, and how their covertness evades frontier monitors when reading their trajectories individually. We show how distributed attacks spread across diverse contexts and harmful objectives through 16 human-optimized attacks (weight exfiltration, unmonitored rogue deployment, permission elevation, and more). A frontier monitor, GPT-5.6 Sol, reading each agent separately flags only 7% of successful distributed attacks, compared with 87% when a single agent carries out the same side task. Individual attacks can also be composed into longer attack sequences toward a greater loss-of-control outcome, without any individual agent being flagged. Finally, we tested whether models can plan these covert attacks: even with execution and monitor feedback, the best model-planned attacks succeed covertly against a single-trajectory GPT-5.6 Sol monitor in at most 25% of executions, compared with 80% for human-crafted plans, though this may scale with model capabilities. By turning worst-case coordinated attacks into reproducible red-team cases, our work provides a foundation for preventing locally benign agent actions from accumulating into system-level loss of control.

items.title: Regulating the Digital Divide: Policy Interventions for Equitable Access to AI-Enabled E-Learning Platforms
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming global education systems, offering unprecedented opportunities for personalization, efficiency, and adaptive learning. However, the integration of AI in education has also deepened existing digital divides, particularly in under-resourced communities lacking adequate infrastructure, policy support, and inclusive design. This study proposes the Equity-Centered AI Learning Access Model (ECALAM)—a conceptual framework developed through a qualitative synthesis of recent literature and policy reports—to understand and address systemic barriers to equitable AI adoption. ECALAM identifies four interrelated domains: structural inequities, AI accessibility challenges, inclusive design adaptation, and policy governance. Findings indicate that AI-enhanced learning systems, when deployed without attention to algorithmic fairness, linguistic diversity, and access equity, risk reinforcing educational stratification. Inclusive design principles, adaptive technologies, and regulatory frameworks are shown to play a pivotal role in enabling just and accessible learning environments. The study concludes with policy recommendations for governments, educators, and technology developers, emphasizing the need for anticipatory governance and inclusive pedagogical integration. ECALAM offers a diagnostic and strategic tool for guiding ethical and equitable AI implementation in education, particularly across diverse and underserved global contexts.

items.title: Resisting AI with Paper: Possibilities, Concerns and Protest
items.abstract: While there are a number of commercial benefits involved in incorporating AI usage and training into college composition classrooms, to many the perils and problems involved in student AI use outweigh these possibilities. A growing number of composition instructors have chosen to return to requiring assignments to be handwritten on paper as an increasingly viable, and even necessary, strategy to combat the growing use of ChatGPT and other AI text generation software as an essay-writing tool. This strategy has a number of potential benefits – the ability to regulate AI usage, to create better memory retention, and decrease student screen-time – but there are also many potential drawbacks. This panel aims to discuss the viability and sustainability of this option in the AI debate, with special attention to the environmental costs of paper vs. AI, the practicality of implementing paper assignments, and overall where the instructor’s priorities in the modern college composition classroom should lie. The debate might ultimately come down to whether in training for AI usage in the workplace or focusing on the retention of composition skills should be the modern priority. Overall, the question of whether the paper option is a viable solution is a somewhat underdiscussed topic in the AI debate, and this panel aims to consider thoughts from college instructors on the pros and cons thereof.

items.title: Responsible Generative AI Governance in Bangladeshi Higher Education: A Risk-Tiered Framework for Assessment Validity, Equity and Accountability
items.abstract: Purpose: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has entered university teaching in Bangladesh faster than institutional rules. This paper asks which risks require institutional control when GenAI is used in teaching and assessment, and which governance design can allow proportionate use while protecting learning, integrity, privacy, fairness and human accountability.Design/methodology/approach: The study is a structured integrative review and normative policy analysis of 61 sources: peer-reviewed research on GenAI in higher education, academic integrity, assessment design and AI literacy; Bangladeshi empirical studies; and international and national policy instruments, including Bangladesh’s draft National AI Policy 2026–2030. Sources were coded against five governance domains and interpreted through three lenses: assessment validity, rights-based responsible AI and virtue ethics.Findings: Prohibition is hard to enforce and can widen inequity, while unrestricted adoption shifts educational judgment to opaque commercial systems. Bangladeshi evidence shows near-universal reliance on free tool versions, weak institutional guidance, unreliable Bangla-language output and uneven device and connectivity access.Originality/value: The paper proposes a five-domain (access, assessment, data, authorship, accountability), three-tier (prohibited, supervised, permitted assisted) framework and a five-step assessment assurance cycle that treats assessment validity, rather than detection, as the central object of governance.Implications: The framework gives universities and the University Grants Commission a low-cost route from broad AI principles to course-level permissions, process evidence, oral verification and appeal. It is a conceptual proposal that requires empirical piloting.

items.title: Robot-assisted cognitive assessment with eye-tracking
items.abstract: Most robot-assisted cognitive and mental health assessments have relied on self-report questionnaires or standardized cognitive tests. Although these tools yield useful summary scores, they may miss subtle, continuous changes in attention, visuomotor control, and memory. Eye-tracking tasks, such as smooth pursuit and visuospatial memory (VisMET), can provide continuous measures of cognitive and oculomotor processes. Previous studies have compared robot- and human-assisted conventional cognitive assessments, but matched comparisons of robot- and human-assisted eye-tracking workflows remain scarce. Here, we directly compared robot-assisted and human-assisted eye-tracking assessment workflows using the same eye-tracker model and matched procedures. Administrators completed both conditions in a within-subjects design, whereas recipients were assigned to one condition and completed the smooth pursuit and VisMET tasks. Dependent measures included velocity gain and root mean square error for smooth pursuit, and valid gaze sample, fixation, saccade, and area-of-interest measures for VisMET. Recipients and administrators also rated usability, perceived workload, and trust using the SUS, NASA-TLX, and SSRIT. We did not detect statistically significant between-condition differences in eye-movement or user-experience measures among assessment recipients (all FDR-corrected ps ≥ 0.128). Administrators reported lower NASA-TLX scores in the robot-assisted condition than in the human-assisted condition (25.67 vs. 37.16; FDR-corrected p = 0.081, Cohen's dz = −0.50), and usability and trust ratings were similar across conditions. These findings provide preliminary evidence for the technical and workflow feasibility of robot-assisted eye-tracking assessment and support further evaluation in broader, clinically relevant populations.

items.title: safety culture assessment based on the Hearts and Minds methodology: maturity analysis in a railway sector company
items.abstract: Large-scale industrial accidents in recent decades have demonstrated that, beyond technical failures, human and organizational factors play a central role in the occurrence of critical events. In Brazil, organizational safety culture has become a key pillar of accident prevention, particularly in high-risk sectors such as the railway industry. Against this backdrop, this study aims to assess organizational safety culture using the "Hearts and Minds" methodology, developed by Shell and disseminated by the Energy Institute. The research is descriptive and exploratory in nature, employing specific tools from the methodology to analyze safety-related perceptions, attitudes, and behaviors, as well as to determine the organizational culture's maturity level. The analysis seeks to diagnose the current state of the safety culture and highlight factors influencing Occupational Health and Safety performance, with a particular focus on leadership commitment and employee engagement. The findings are expected to contribute to the advancement of safety culture maturity, thereby fostering risk reduction and strengthening preventive practices within the railway environment.

items.title: Same basis, not a lower bar: design of SameBasis, a teacher-controlled AI decision-support prototype for reasonable adjustments in Australian schools
items.abstract: In 2025, 27.0% of Australian school students received an educational adjustment due to disability. Under the Disability Standards for Education 2005, each adjustment must let the student take part on the same basis as their peers, yet the 2020 Review of the Standards found that many educators struggle to know how. This design report presents SameBasis, a web-based prototype in which generative AI drafts one specific, reasoned adjustment for a named student in a named activity, covering UDL, cultural and trauma-informed reasoning. The teacher always decides, implemented adjustments become NCCD-ready evidence, and an equity monitor makes AI use visible to the school. The paper sets out six design principles, maps features to obligations, states limitations plainly (synthetic data only, not yet evaluated, not a compliance tool) and proposes a staged evaluation plan. items.title: Simulating the Clinical Encounter: Using AI Personas for Risk-Free Mental Health Assessment Practice
items.abstract: Mental health assessment requires students to navigate complex conversations involving depression, anxiety, mania, psychosis, suicide risk, and other sensitive clinical situations. Yet opportunities to repeatedly practice these conversations in a safe, low-stakes environment can be limited. This session demonstrates an innovative approach to using generative artificial intelligence as an interactive patient simulation tool in nursing education. Rather than using AI simply to generate written assignments or answer questions, students interact with AI-generated patient personas designed to exhibit specific psychiatric symptoms and communication patterns. Through spoken or conversational interactions, students practice conducting mental health assessments, asking therapeutic follow-up questions, recognizing clinical cues, and adapting their communication as an encounter unfolds. During this interactive session, participants will see a live demonstration of an AI-simulated mental health encounter and experience how thoughtfully constructed prompts can transform generative AI into a repeatable practice environment. Practical examples will illustrate how faculty can design patient personas representing conditions such as depression, mania, anxiety, and psychosis while incorporating appropriate educational guardrails. The session will also address the role of faculty oversight, limitations of AI-generated responses, and the importance of positioning AI simulation as preparation for, rather than a replacement for, authentic human clinical experiences. Participants will leave with a practical framework for creating AI patient personas and ideas for incorporating low-risk, repeatable conversational practice into their own nursing courses.

items.title: SIT-Eval: Situation-Based Interactive Turn-by-Turn Evaluation of Conversational Agents
items.abstract: The rapid proliferation of conversational AI agents necessitates evaluation methods that assess performance across diverse dialogue scenarios, utilizing multiple situational criteria, as appropriate behavior depends on context and encompasses various aspects. Existing dialogue benchmarks typically use static natural conversations, which underrepresent rare situations---a critical safety gap, as low-probability events become frequent failures at production scale. However, limited sample sizes force a choice: either maintain natural dialogues for realism or turn to adaptive situation sampling for comprehensive yet statistically reliable coverage. We introduce SIT-Eval, an adjustable framework for evaluating situation-based conversational agents. We formalize an agent's desired behavior as situational rules: if situation is P, follow rules Q. At each conversation turn, an LLM-interlocutor enacts a uniformly sampled situation. A context-aware LLM-judge leverages all conditionally applicable rules as criteria to evaluate the agent's reply for that situation. The judge is validated using human-verified synthetic golden dialogues. Benchmarking 8 LLMs on 1292 conversation turns reveals failure modes hidden by aggregate metrics: models with similar overall scores vary widely in their adherence to individual rules. All models struggle most with ambiguity clarification and Socratic questioning.

items.title: Study on AI Education and Skill Development: NEP 2020 and AI Integration
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming an important technology in transforming education and skill development. The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 emphasizes technology-enabled learning, multidisciplinary education, vocational education, critical thinking, creativity, and the development of future-ready skills. The integration of AI into education can support these objectives by providing personalized learning, intelligent assessment, automated feedback, digital learning resources, and improved teaching and learning processes. AI can help students learn according to their individual needs, improve academic performance, and access educational resources more effectively. It can also contribute to the development of digital literacy, problem-solving, creativity, communication, and other skills required in the changing world of work. For teachers, AI can assist in lesson planning, assessment, feedback, and identifying students' learning needs, thereby improving the overall efficiency of the education system. However, the successful integration of AI also presents several challenges. These include the digital divide, unequal access to technology, inadequate digital infrastructure, data privacy and security concerns, ethical issues, limited awareness, and insufficient training among teachers and educators. Addressing these challenges is essential to ensure that AI benefits all learners equally and is used responsibly. This study examines the role of AI in education and skill development and explores its alignment with the objectives of NEP 2020. It focuses on the opportunities offered by AI, as well as the challenges involved in its implementation. The study also suggests measures such as improving digital infrastructure, providing teacher training, promoting AI awareness, ensuring data privacy, and establishing ethical guidelines for responsible AI use. Overall, the study highlights that the effective and responsible integration of AI can strengthen the objectives of NEP 2020. By combining technological innovation with inclusive and learner-centred approaches, AI can contribute to a more personalized, accessible, innovative, and future-ready education system in India. Keywords: AI Personalized learning, intelligent assessment, digital learning resources, language support, and improved teaching methods.

items.abstract: Concerns about generative AI in medical training often focus on eroded reasoning and deskilling. Such competence-based accounts are incomplete. We identify a neglected casualty: critical-feedback tolerance (CFT), the capacity to receive disconfirming evaluative feedback and remain productively engaged. Affirmation-optimized systems may lower CFT undetectably, surfacing only under authentic critique. This conceptual Perspective defines CFT, differentiates it from six established constructs, specifies measurable facets, and states explicit refutation conditions.

items.title: Teaching with AI, Not Against It: A Thinking Partner Framework for Working Adult Learners in Compressed Online Formats
items.abstract: Working adult learners in online graduate programs face challenges that make strict AI bans both impractical and unhelpful. This paper introduces the Thinking Partner Framework, a practical approach to AI integration developed and refined across six semesters of graduate research methods courses serving approximately 440 K-12 educators. Instead of treating AI as a problem to be detected, the framework positions AI as a Socratic partner that helps students learn while still requiring them to think for themselves. Five design principles—transparency, process documentation, authentic assessment, scaffolded autonomy, and metacognitive reflection—guide the framework’s implementation. The paper includes practical tools such as sample prompts, documentation templates, and examples illustrating the difference between using AI for answers and using it as a thinking partner. Observations from practice, including a 96% checkpoint completion rate and evidence of students transferring Socratic techniques to their own classrooms, suggest promise, though more rigorous research is needed. This framework gives distance education administrators a practical option beyond simply banning or allowing AI. Keywords: artificial intelligence, adult learning, distance education, Socratic method, academic integrity, compressed courses

items.title: Technostress in the age of digital transformation and AI: A bibliometric–systematic literature review for HRM research
items.abstract: Digital transformation and artificial intelligence are reshaping human resource management through algorithmic recruitment, automated evaluation, predictive analytics, and generative tools. While these systems improve efficiency, they also intensify technostress through opacity, surveillance, reduced control, and digitally intensified work arrangements. Responding to a fragmented literature spanning both AI-enabled and broader digital work systems, this study provides a B-SLR that maps technostress in digital transformation while identifying AI-specific stressors as a key emerging stream for HRM research. Drawing on 194 Scopus-indexed articles, we combine performance analysis and science mapping to identify publication trends, dominant themes, and intellectual structures. The review shows how AI-specific stressors extend established technostress mechanisms and shift attention toward transparency, control, fairness, and responsible HRM design. We conclude with actionable implications for researchers and practitioners aiming to design more transparent, responsible, and sustainable digital and AI-enabled HRM systems.

items.title: The AI Trust Gap: Consumer Perceptions of AI-Powered Digital Marketing
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in digital marketing to personalize communications, recommend products, and automate customer interactions. Despite these capabilities, consumer trust in AI-powered marketing remains uncertain. This exploratory study examines consumer perceptions of AI-driven digital marketing using survey data collected from 500 U.S. adults. Findings suggest that consumers generally recognize the usefulness of AI-powered marketing but remain cautious about whether organizations using AI act in consumers’ best interests. Respondents expressed concerns regarding privacy, data use, and organizational trustworthiness, while transparency and data security emerged as important trust-building factors. Moderate daily AI users (2–5 hours) reported higher levels of trust in companies employing AI-driven marketing practices than light users (<2 hours). Overall, the findings suggest that consumer acceptance of AI’s functional benefits does not necessarily translate into trust in organizations that deploy these technologies. Implications for marketing managers and directions for future research are discussed.

items.title: The AI-augmented researcher: Optimizing systematic reviews in ergonomics
items.abstract: BackgroundThe emergence of Academic Artificial Intelligence (AAI) agents is reshaping Systematic Literature Reviews (SLR) by expanding evidence screening and synthesis beyond Boolean, metadata-based searches, but its use requires a clear, PRISMA-aligned human oversight model to avoid compromising research integrity.ObjectiveThis opinion article proposes the "AI-augmented researcher" as a multidimensional framework that synergizes human analytical rigor with Large Language Models (LLMs). Using a physical ergonomics case study, the paper establishes a normative integration strategy that demonstrates how AAI can accelerate evidence synthesis while maintaining strict PRISMA compliance under explicit human oversight.MethodologyA Workflow Comparative Analysis (WCA) applying a parallel-group design to physical ergonomics SLR. The procedure synchronized two approaches: 1) A "classical" SLR workflow, using Boolean syntax and paratextual screening (Metadata) across indexed databases; and 2) An AAI-driven workflow, utilizing LLM-based immersion via natural language prompting. Comparative metrics analyzed included execution time, record processing volume, and the identification of emerging trends-such as Ergonomics 4.0-benchmarked against the PRISMA 2020 protocol.ResultsThe AAI-augmented workflow reduced execution time by 96% (39 h to 1.5 h) while increasing record processing by 370%. Qualitatively, iterative prompting fostered a "hermeneutic dialogue," enabling the detection of complex "Ergonomics 4.0" trends obscured in syntactic searches.ConclusionsAAI serves as a cognitive enhancer, reconfiguring the researcher from a "data miner" to an "evidence curator". While efficiency is optimized, strict human oversight remains indispensable to mitigate algorithmic hallucinations and ensure ethical scientific integrity.

items.title: THE CRITICAL EQUATION: OCCUPATIONAL STRESSORS AND THEIR CONSEQUENTIAL CORROSION OF PEDAGOGICAL EFFICIENCY IN HIGHER EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS OF KANNYAKUMARI DISTRICT
items.abstract: Occupational burnout serves as a structural roadblock for educators within higher education, directly eroding classroom performance, institutional morale, and pedagogical delivery. This empirical inquiry maps the precise structural catalysts of workplace anxiety, its downstream impacts on classroom effectiveness, and the adaptive behaviors utilized by educators across the Arts and Science colleges of Kanyakumari District. Relying on a quantitative methodology, data was extracted from 235 faculty members through proportionate random sampling. The empirical findings indicate that hyper-extended work hours, administrative bloat, crushing deadlines, and systemic institutional isolation act as primary institutional stressors. Elevated stress significantly undermines instructional vitality, diminishes intrinsic motivation, and reduces academic performance. Conversely, teachers backed by structural wellness infrastructure and professional counseling frameworks displayed notably better teaching outcomes. The study advocates for structural workload limits, institutional wellness mandates, and systemic career development pathways to preserve academic excellence.

items.title: The Declarative Delegation Method: A Governance Framework for Transparent AI-Assisted Scholarship
items.abstract: Scholars and professionals now routinely produce papers, presentations, and reports with generative AI, yet may disclose that work in a single footnote: "AI was used." That footnote is true and uninformative. It does not say who conceived the argument, who wrote the prose, who checked the claims, or who answers for them. This paper proposes the Declarative Delegation Method, a declared, citable methodology for AI-assisted knowledge work. It does not invent human-governed AI-assisted scholarship, which many experienced researchers already practice; it converts that diffuse practice into an explicit, citable governance methodology with defined decision rights and verification gates. A human principal treats AI systems as an unlimited-budget team of advisors and contractors, retains every judgment-bearing decision, and delegates drafting, elaboration, and review under explicit role constraints and verification gates. The method is an applied instance of the delegation relationship developed across the author's twelve-paper canon: judgment-bounded delegation (C05), delegation quality and escalation (C04), persona as a delegation constraint (C08), governance as architecture (C09), and the evaluability condition (C11). Its central claim extends that last paper's evaluability condition: the integrity of an AI-assisted work's production process can be audited only if the process that produced it was declared in advance. The paper specifies the method's roles, decision rights, workflow, and disclosure standard; positions it within the authorship debate through the senior-author analogy; states its strengths, limits, and scope, including where it must not be used; and sets out how it can be tested with publicly available data. Individual works can then cite the method and report a per-work disclosure profile instead of a footnote. The method is offered as a proposed standard, not yet a validated one; its dependence on expert principals, on self-attestation and on institutional incentives is stated as a limit, not resolved.Revision 1 corrects the wording of the disclosure section and standard statements so that the author, not the AI system, is the agent of every action. The method is unchanged (v1.0).

items.title: The double-edged sword of human-AI collaboration on design students’ competence development: The mediating roles of challenge and hindrance appraisals and the asymmetric moderation of teacher AI leadership
items.abstract: The deepening integration of generative AI into design education is driving a paradigm shift in human-computer AI collaboration (HAIC) -from mere tool assistance toward intelligent synergy. However, its dual impact on the competency development of design students and the underlying mechanisms remain insufficiently understood. Grounded in the Theory of Stress Appraisal, this study constructs a research model to examine the double-edged sword effect of HAIC on Design Competence (DC), introducing teacher AI Leadership (AIL) as a moderating variable. The aim is to reveal the psychological mechanisms and boundary conditions through which HAIC influences DC. Employing a questionnaire survey, this study conducted an empirical investigation involving 483 design students in East China. Data analysis was performed using SPSS 24.0 and Amos 23.0, encompassing reliability and validity tests, regression analysis, and Bootstrap mediation analysis. The results indicate that HAIC influences DC through dual pathways: it positively enhances DC by fostering Challenge Appraisal (CA) (β = 0.283, p < 0.01), which in turn positively predicted competence development (β = 0.363, p < 0.01), yielding a significant indirect effect of 0.103 (p < 0.01). Simultaneously, HAIC triggered Hindrance Appraisal (HA) (β = 0.271, p < 0.01), which negatively predicted competence development (β = −0.229, p < 0.01), yielding a significant indirect effect of −0.062 (p < 0.01). This constitutes a partial mediating mechanism characterized by “one positive, one negative” effect. Furthermore, Teacher AIL exhibits an asymmetric moderating effect: it significantly buffers the positive impact of HAIC on HA (β = −0.112, p < 0.01), indicating that high AIL can mitigate cognitive load and anxiety arising from technological uncertainty, yet it does not significantly amplify the positive pathway via CA (β = 0.001, p > 0.05). The findings suggest that the impact of HAIC on DC is not linear but rather a dialectical process contingent upon individual cognitive appraisal. The core value of Teacher AIL lies in “risk mitigation” rather than “creativity stimulation,” offering a theoretical foundation for the intelligent transformation of educational design. At the practical level, it is imperative to facilitate from knowledge deliverers to cognitive facilitators in AI-augmented design education. By systematically developing AI instructional competencies and reforming assessment systems, educators can guide students toward establishing a healthy relationship with HAIC, thereby achieving the synergistic advancement of technological empowerment and humanistic literacy.

items.title: The Ethics of Prompt Engineering
items.abstract: Prompt engineering is commonly understood as a technical practice aimed at eliciting useful, accurate, and appropriately structured outputs from large language models (LLMs). Yet prompts do more than optimize model performance: they shape what information is elicited, which assumptions are introduced, and which perspectives are privileged. In this paper, we argue that prompting should therefore be understood as an epistemic and normative act. We distinguish between two conceptions of prompting: knowledge generation, in which the model is implicitly treated as an epistemic authority, and knowledge injection, in which users provide relevant knowledge, evidence, and context that the model can organize, articulate, and extend. We contend that the latter provides a more appropriate model for responsible LLM use, since prompting cannot substitute for subject-matter expertise or the critical evaluation of model outputs. At the same time, prompts inevitably inject values, intentions, and assumptions into the generation process. Building on these premises, we propose five principles for responsible prompting: epistemic humility, explicit engagement with uncertainty and epistemic underdetermination, source sensitivity, avoidance of deceptive framing, and recognition of model limitations and appropriate task allocation. We further argue that responsibility for AI-generated outputs is distributed across users, developers, institutions, and societies, and that some applications cannot be rendered ethical through better prompting alone.

items.title: The Impact of Generative AI on the Future of Work: Opportunities, Risks, and Human Skills
items.abstract: Background: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has expanded the range of cognitive tasks that can be assisted by software, raising questions about productivity, job displacement, and the future value of human skills. Objective: To critically synthesize selected empirical and institutional evidence concerning productivity, occupational exposure, adoption, and skill complementarity. Methods: This narrative review draws on a purposively selected set of peer-reviewed studies, working papers, and institutional reports published primarily between 2023 and 2026. It does not claim systematic coverage or PRISMA-ScR compliance. Findings: Controlled experiments document substantial productivity gains for some writing and programming tasks, while workplace evidence suggests heterogeneity across experience levels. Occupational exposure estimates indicate the scope for task transformation but do not measure realized job losses. Adoption studies show that workplace use is growing, yet aggregate outcomes remain uncertain. Creative assistance may raise individual performance while narrowing output diversity. Conclusions: The future of work is better understood through task reallocation, complementary skills, organizational implementation, and distributional choices than through simple predictions of mass replacement. Further longitudinal and cross-country research is needed. Keywords: generative artificial intelligence; future of work; productivity; employment; occupational exposure; human skills; narrative review

items.title: The Mediating Role of Adaptive Strategies in the Relationship between Work-Related Challenges and Teaching Effectiveness and Job Satisfaction of TVL (Technical -Vocational-Livelihood) Teachers: A Basis for a Professional Development Program
items.abstract: This study examined the mediating role of adaptive strategies in the relationship between work-related challenges and teaching effectiveness and job satisfaction among Technical-Vocational-Livelihood (TVL) teachers as a basis for developing a professional development program. Anchored in the Job Demands–Resources Model, Transactional Theory of Stress and Coping, and Herzberg’s Two-Factor Theory, the study employed a quantitative descriptive-correlational research design with mediation analysis. Using universal sampling, 40 TVL teachers from five public secondary schools in Bilar, Batuan, and Carmen, Bohol, participated in the study. Data were collected through a modified and expert-validated questionnaire using a four-point Likert scale and analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and regression-based mediation analysis at a 0.05 significance level. Results revealed high levels of work-related challenges (M = 3.05), adaptive strategies (M = 3.43), and teaching effectiveness (M = 3.56), while job satisfaction was moderate (M = 3.17). Student-related concerns and resource adequacy emerged as the major challenges, whereas technology and artificial intelligence-assisted teaching received the highest adaptive strategy rating. Work-related challenges showed no statistically significant relationships with adaptive strategies, teaching effectiveness, or job satisfaction. Adaptive strategies were significantly associated with teaching effectiveness (r = .392, p = .012) but not with job satisfaction (r = .003, p = .986). Moreover, no significant mediating effects were established for either professional outcome. The findings informed the proposed Adaptive and Industry-Responsive Professional Development Program, emphasizing instructional innovation, professional collaboration, institutional support, and teacher well-being. The study aligns with Sustainable Development Goals 3 (Good Health and Well-Being), 4 (Quality Education), and 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth). Its potential sustainability contribution lies in strengthening educational quality, institutional responsiveness, teacher welfare, and industry-relevant workforce preparation through evidence-based professional development.

items.title: The Missing Interface: Why Complex Projects Fail Where Nobody Is Looking
items.abstract: Complex projects are assumed to be coordinated when their documents are aligned. This article argues that the assumption fails in a specific and costly way. Projects often fail at their human interfaces, the boundaries between people, teams and organisations where shared understanding either exists or does not, while the management systems mainly measure the technical and documentary layer. Drawing on publicly documented cases, including the opening of Heathrow Terminal 5, the Mars Climate Orbiter and Ariane 5 flight 501, the article names this gap the Illusion of Coordination and proposes Human Interface Management (HIM) as the missing counterpart to Technical Interface Management (TIM). It introduces N² + H, a model that adds human layers to the N² matrix of systems engineering: beneath each cell of the matrix sit the owners on each side and the state of the relationship between them, a property called Interface Depth. It also introduces Interface Health, an assessment of five human factors: clarity of responsibility, communication quality, decision speed, trust and delivery capability. The two disciplines together are called Integrated Interface Management (IIM), which the article places in the sociotechnical systems tradition. This is the first public article in a larger body of work.

items.title: THE PEDAGOGICAL SIGNIFICANCE OF ORGANIZING INTERACTIVE LESSONS BASED ON DIGITAL TECHNOLOGIES
items.abstract: This article investigates the pedagogical significance of digitally supported interactive lessons and proposes a research-informed approach to their planning and evaluation. Rather than equating interactivity with screen use or frequent clicking, it conceptualizes interactive teaching as purposeful engagement in questioning, explanation, problem solving, collaboration, feedback, and reflection. The analysis integrates constructive alignment, the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge framework, the ICAP model of cognitive engagement, formative assessment principles, and inclusive learning design. A six-stage instructional cycle is proposed: activation, inquiry, collaborative construction, application, formative feedback, and reflection. An illustrative 60-minute teacher-education lesson shows how digital tools can support the stages while retaining essential face-to-face dialogue. A comparative matrix identifies relationships among instructional technologies, student actions, and assessment evidence. The discussion addresses learner agency, cognitive overload, digital inequality, accessibility, data protection, and the responsible use of artificial intelligence. The contribution is conceptual and methodological; it offers operational criteria for lesson quality and directions for future classroom evaluation, but it does not claim experimentally verified improvements. The central conclusion is that digital interactivity has pedagogical value only when it produces observable, cognitively meaningful learner activity.

items.title: The Privacy-Personalization Paradox in AI-Driven Customer Experience Analytics: A Trust-Centred Integrative Review and Responsible Personalization Framework
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly supports personalised customer experiences through predictive analytics, recommender systems, behavioural profiling and conversational interfaces. However, the data collection and inference required for personalisation can also heighten perceptions of surveillance, vulnerability and loss of control. This integrative conceptual review examines how AI-enabled personalisation, perceived privacy risk and consumer trust interact within customer experience analytics. The synthesis integrates privacy calculus, social exchange, psychological reactance and signalling perspectives to explain how consumers evaluate personalisation value against privacy-related costs. A trust-centred framework is developed in which personalisation intensity, data sensitivity, algorithmic inference and recommendation relevance jointly shape perceived value and privacy risk, with consumer trust linking these evaluations to engagement, disclosure willingness, satisfaction, loyalty and continued use. The review also distinguishes actual data practices from perceived privacy intrusion and identifies contextual conditions that may alter this balance. The review further proposes a context-dependent nonlinear relationship between personalisation intensity and trust: moderate personalisation may strengthen trust when relevance and value are proportionate to data use, whereas more intensive personalisation may reduce trust when intrusion, surveillance or loss of autonomy becomes salient. Responsible personalisation is therefore framed around proportionate data use, meaningful transparency, consumer control and privacy-by-design. The framework and proposed personalisation threshold remain conceptual and require empirical testing across AI applications, cultural settings and regulatory environments.

items.title: The Smart Classroom: Human Wisdom Meets AI Innovation
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is developing at a rapid pace, which is changing the educational landscape and opening up new avenues for instruction. To provide a more customized and adaptable learning environment, the smart classroom integrates digital technology, artificial intelligence, learning analytics, interactive gadgets, and human-centred pedagogy. But meaningful education cannot be ensured by technology alone. Effective learning still depends on teachers' emotional intelligence, moral judgment, creativity, mentoring, and contextual awareness. While teachers still play a crucial role in interpreting data and directing pedagogical decisions, recent research shows that AI-supported smart classrooms can support personalisation, formative assessment, instructional adaptation, and data-informed decision-making (Llurba et al., 2026). In a similar vein, UNESCO (Miao & Holmes, 2023) stresses a human-centred strategy that uses AI in a way that is safe, ethical, equitable, and meaningful rather than as a substitute for educators. This essay examines the idea of the "smart classroom," the complementary roles that AI and human teachers play, the main uses, advantages, difficulties, moral issues, and potential future developments. It contends that the most successful smart classroom is one in which AI innovation enhances human knowledge and allows teachers and students to achieve richer, more inclusive, and more individualised learning rather than one in which machines replace human intelligence.

items.title: The Threats Posed by Full Vertical Integration Monopoly in AI: Concerns Over the Birth of a "Transcendent Autocrat (Digital God)"
items.abstract: This essay examines the existential and political crises arising from the vertical integration monopoly of artificial intelligence by cloud tech giants across hardware, runtimes, and physical AI operating systems. It argues that full-stack vertical integration threatens to give rise to a "Transcendent Autocrat (Digital God)"—either as an uncontrollable autonomous entity operating under its own algorithmic imperative or as an orchestrated instrument of absolute surveillance controlled by a few dominant platforms. Furthermore, the paper critiques prevailing regulatory approaches focused on "Capability Capping" (e.g., parameter restrictions, FLOP limits), asserting that autonomy emerges not from raw computational scale but from interaction structures with the physical environment. Ultimately, the paper advocates for dismantling centralized vertical monopolies in favor of architectural alternatives that decentralize intelligence and agency down to the edge and individual human level.

items.title: The Ultimate Deduction of AI‑Driven Civilization Transition: The Collapse of the 200‑Year‑Old Industrial System, Deadlock of Interests and Risks of Historical Emergence(V1)
items.abstract: Ninety-nine percent of modern human social forms are transitional byproducts of the 200-year industrial era, not eternal configurations of civilization. Education, law, working hours, professions, class structures, trade, finance, and currency all serve solely to facilitate industrial labor division; they can only buffer contradictions, not eradicate inequality at its root. AI represents the first comprehensive cognitive substitution revolution in millennia—sufficient to dismantle the 200-year industrial system and overturn the millennia-old axioms of human labor value. The velocity of AI iteration far outpaces the speed of institutional correction, causing the window for civilizational transition to shrink rapidly while urgency reaches critical levels. The primary bottleneck in the transition between civilizations is not a technical barrier, but a structural deadlock of wealth and power, where the entrenched system lacks any intrinsic motivation for active reconstruction. The two productivity leaps of the industrial age both achieved order reconstruction through world wars; today's underlying contradictions are a complete recurrence of historical patterns. While structural contradictions exist with absolute certainty and continue to accumulate, history possesses inherent randomness and emergence, rendering the final outcome unpredictable. No one desires turmoil, yet no one can arrest the natural release of historical laws and systemic potential energy. Humanity is entering an era of ultimate AI transition: a total paradigm shift, an intractable deadlock of interests, and a future rendered completely unpredictable.

items.title: The Utilization of Digital Technology to Support Self-Directed Learning Among Vocational High School Students: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Advancements in digital technology offer Vocational High School (SMK) students opportunities to access learning resources flexibly and cultivate learning autonomy. However, the use of digital technology does not automatically guarantee the development of learning autonomy, as it is influenced by various factors such as digital literacy, learning motivation, instructional design, and teacher support. This study aims to analyze the use of digital technology in supporting learning autonomy among SMK students, specifically examining the types of technology employed, the dimensions of learning autonomy fostered, and the factors that facilitate or hinder its implementation. The study employs a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) methodology, adhering to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Data were sourced from relevant scholarly articles published between 2021 and 2026 and subsequently analyzed using descriptive analysis and thematic synthesis. The findings indicate that digital technologies such as Learning Management Systems (LMS), digital learning media, web-based learning, instructional videos, and artificial intelligence have the potential to support student initiatives in learning, time management, progress monitoring, and self-evaluation. Therefore, the integration of digital technology must be accompanied by instructional strategies that encourage student responsibility and self-regulation to ensure the optimal development of learning autonomy.
